newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn tiptoes back into long end of debt mkt.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn tiptoes back into long end of debt mkt.

text.p: Eager to spread the burden of its debt further along the yield curve, the German government on Monday said it would issue its first 30-year bond since three-and-a-half-years ago.

Even as the government's issuance plans had been well advertised with a number of public statements, the news nonetheless left markets slightly jittery that the issue could signal an end to Germany's five-year easing cycle.
Bonn will issue the 30-year bond through the federal bond consortium and an auction on July 1 and 2.

"One can't help but have a slightly uncomfortable feeling," Trinkaus Capital Management bond analyst Frank Schroeder said, explaining Bonn would surely not lock itself into these rates for 30 years if it expected interest rates to fall further.

Traders also admitted to pangs of nervousness, remembering Germany's last ill-fated 30-year bond -- the New Year 1993/1994 issue -- and looking at a number of inflationary risks littering the way ahead.
"We will greet the new 30-year bond with a bit of fear, largely because of painful memories associated with Bonn's last issuance of a long-dated bond," a Frankfurt-based trader said.

To be fair, analysts said a series of U.S. interest rate hikes were more directly responsible for the bond markets' meltdown in spring 1994 than the 30-year Bund. Conditions were very different now, ensuring Bonn's new issue should not be perceived as quite the same disaster this time.

"It wasn't the 30-year which switched off the bond markets' lights," recalled Ros Lifton, economist at HSBC Markets in London, stressing: "Now one Fed rate hike may be priced in, but the market surely is not looking for a series of rate rises."

Since Germany's main reason for testing the waters at the long end is to finally lengthen its formerly compact capital market, rich with 10-year debt, Bonn took pains to eliminate any element of potential surprise.
Germany plans to allow bond-stripping which necessitates longer-dated securities, traders said.
"Bonn and the Bundesbank did the utmost to give plenty of warning," and clearly defined the plans, Lifton said.
In fact dealers said the shock would have been far greater had Bonn now scrapped its plans to issue a 30-year bond.

Beyond effective advertising about the issue's existence, Bonn also limited the issue's volume to around 10 billion marks, far below market expectations for 15-20 billion marks, to help ensure success.

"I think it is fair to say that we expect good demand for this bond," said Laurent Sransolet, bond analyst at J.P. Morgan in Brussels. He said demand should be relatively high because no 10-year issue is scheduled for the third quarter.
While expecting the issue to be a success, dealers said they did not forecast aggressive bidding during the auction.
One problem Bonn was not able to cater for is the timing of the issue, analysts said, agreeing it would be an ominous date, several days before critical U.S. June employment figures.
But even if there is nervousness before the U.S. data, which is sure to provide one more clue as to whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates again, the German 30-issue should not flop.
"It will probably be a nice German 30 year issue, not too boring but also not too exciting," Lifton said.
